title: Warming Trends on the Hurd Peninsula of Livingston Island, Antarctica, Between 2000 and 2024, and Improvements in the Estimation of Air Temperature Using C6.1 MODIS LST Data
content: Analysing the spatial and temporal variability of near-surface air temperature (Ta) is essential for assessing climate change, particularly in polar regions such as the maritime Antarctic, where observational studies remain comparatively scarce. In areas with sparse meteorological networks, satellite observations provide a valuable means of extending station-based analyses and generating spatially distributed Ta maps. This study analyses updated Ta records from six meteorological stations on the Hurd Peninsula, Livingston Island, for 2000–2024, with particular attention to temperature changes since 2016, and evaluates Ta estimation models based on MODIS Terra daytime LST Collection 6.1 data. The analysis of the Ta time series showed significant warming over the complete 2000–2024 period, with trends ranging from 0.53 to 1.27 °C decade−1, and a clear shift towards warming after 2016. While the 2000–2015 period showed spatially contrasting trends, including cooling at JCI, positive trends were observed at all analysed stations during 2016–2024, ranging from 0.40 to 1.33 °C decade−1 and highlighting substantial local variability across the Hurd Peninsula. The global Ta model, developed using data from all six stations and based on MODIS Terra daytime LST and spatiotemporal variables, achieved a performance comparable to that obtained with Collection 6, with R2 = 0.77 and a cross-validated RMSE of 2.23 °C. The results also showed that rigorous filtering of the MODIS LST observations is essential: retaining only good-quality data and excluding observations with |view angle| > 45° substantially reduced dispersion in the Ta–LST relationship and removed unrealistically low LST values. The introduction of this view-angle threshold represents a new filtering step with respect to our previous studies.
